rationale:
Evidence: iteration 6 is the best design at 945.4. Oval, s-bend and slalom all finish 20/20 with progress about 0.996 to 0.998 and rms_error 0.006. Remaining gaps, in score terms: completion time (oval 1.99 s, s-bend 2.38 s, slalom 2.57 s, worth 60*(1-t/3) per run, so about 2 points per 0.1 s), line-loss events (about 0.3 to 0.5 per run, worth about 15 points each), and steering oscillation. Iterations 4 to 5 showed that cutting yaw inertia and mass improved results far more than gain changes, and kd is at a plateau. The cleanest next lever is a small speed increase, which is the main source of time savings, and a further mass reduction, which also helps acceleration and turn-back.

Changes: (1) mass 0.6 to 0.5 kg, lowering yaw inertia and improving acceleration, the same direction as the iteration 4 to 5 change that helped. (2) base_speed 0.9 to 0.95, a small step to cut completion time by roughly 4 to 5 percent. I deliberately avoid a larger step: iteration 1 at base_speed 1.0 with a longer body went off track. Sensors, sensor_size 0.016, kp 4.5, ki 0.05, kd 1.0, body, wheels and line_loss stay the same, so the effect is attributable to speed and mass.

Hypotheses: (H1) Lower mass lets the robot reach the higher speed without more off-track events. (H2) Completion time falls by about 0.1 to 0.15 s on the slalom and s-bend, adding roughly 5 to 10 points. Risk: higher speed on slalom could raise max_error toward 0.06 and line losses. If line losses rise or any track drops below 100 percent completion, the next step is to return base_speed to 0.9 and keep only the mass change.

Measurements wanted: completion and completion_time per track, line_loss_events and max_error on slalom, and steering_oscillation to check whether the higher speed or lighter body adds jitter.
